book.title: Factfulness
book.author: Hans Rosling (with Ola Rosling and Anna Rosling Rönnlund)

confidence_note: Rosling's fact questions, the chimpanzee comparison, and the systematic pessimism of answers are central to the book. The book's questions include the share of one-year-olds vaccinated, the change in extreme poverty over 20 years, and global life expectancy. The chimpanzee point is a thought experiment about random guessing, not a real test with chimpanzees. Rosling calls the underlying cause the 'overdramatic worldview' and breaks it into ten instincts; the reference text's single 'drama instinct' label is simplified. Specific percentages of correct answers per group are omitted.
facts: Rosling and his team asked thousands of people in many countries, including highly educated audiences, experts, and leaders, multiple-choice questions about basic global trends, each with three answer options.

Questions included what share of the world's one-year-olds are vaccinated, whether extreme poverty has roughly halved, doubled, or stayed the same over 20 years, and what global life expectancy is today.
Because each question had three options, a chimpanzee picking at random would average about a third correct; most human groups scored worse than that.
The wrong answers were not random: people consistently picked the most negative option, believing the world is poorer, sicker, and more dangerous than it is.

Being better educated or more informed did not protect people; Rosling argues the cause is not a lack of knowledge but an 'overdramatic worldview' shaped by instincts and by news that favours the dramatic.
tension: Educated, well-informed people did worse than random guessing, and always in the same gloomy direction.
opening_idea: Rosling asks a room of experts a simple three-option question about vaccination rates, and then compares their score with what a chimpanzee would get by picking at random.

lessons.idea: Errors that all lean one way point to a bias, not a gap in knowledge.
Expertise and education don't automatically correct a distorted worldview.
lessons.anchor: Highly educated audiences also scored below chance

lessons.idea: A dramatic picture of the world pushes out slow, steady improvements.

reflect: When you last formed a view on how the world is doing, where did the information come from?
Which trend do you feel sure about but have never actually checked?
reflect_final: Next time you catch yourself saying 'things are getting worse', look up the actual trend once before repeating it, and notice whether your guess leaned negative.

use_cases.situation: A dinner conversation turns to how everything in the world is getting worse.
use_cases.move: Mention Rosling's chimpanzee comparison and ask the table to guess the share of the world's one-year-olds who are vaccinated before anyone looks it up.

use_cases.situation: A team is making assumptions about customers or a market based on impressions.
use_cases.move: Ask which assumptions have been checked against data and pick one to verify before the next meeting.

use_cases.situation: You feel gloomy after reading the news.
use_cases.move: Choose one topic from the news and look up its long-term trend rather than the latest headline.

pocket_idea: If your mistakes all lean the same way, it isn't ignorance: it's a worldview tilted toward drama.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: On Rosling's basic questions about the world, a chimpanzee picking at random would beat most experts.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Rosling asked thousands of educated people three-option questions like how many of the world's children are vaccinated; most scored below random chance, and their mistakes all tilted toward a worse world than the real one.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Is there something about the world you were sure was getting worse, and then found out wasn't?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: What people believe about the world versus what the numbers actually show.
